summary: Describes a backward-compatible technique for OSPF routers to advertise that they should not carry transit traffic, or that paths through them are less preferred. It was replaced by RFC 6987.

plainLanguage.summary: A router puts up a sign saying please don't send through traffic my way right now, I'm busy.

questions: how to drain traffic from an ospf router
what is lsinf infinity in ospf
subtitle: Let a router tell others not to send transit traffic through it

tldr.problem: OSPF networks have no standard way for a router to tell others not to use it as a transit point, even though situations like high CPU load or maintenance windows make this necessary.
tldr.mechanism: A router advertises its router-LSA with very high costs on all non-local links. Other routers then prefer alternate paths, while still being able to reach this router's own addresses.
tldr.outcome: It was replaced by RFC 6987, which provides similar functionality.

today: RFC 3137 was obsoleted by RFC 6987, which standardizes OSPF stub router functionality.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
In an OSPF network, routers forward packets destined for other routers and networks by computing shortest paths. Sometimes a router needs to stop forwarding transit traffic while remaining part of the network. This might happen when a router is CPU-bound, running low on memory, or being gracefully introduced to or removed from the network.

The RFC notes that simply removing the router from the network topology by flushing its router-LSA does not work because then other routers cannot reach the router's own IP addresses. The solution keeps the router in the topology but marks it as a stub router that should not carry transit traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A router needs to say I am still here and you can reach me, but please do not send traffic through me to other places right now.

sections.title: The Stub Router Solution
sections.content:
The solution modifies how the stub router advertises its router-LSA. Links of type three (stub links, which connect to directly attached networks) keep their normal interface costs. All other links get set to LSInfinity, a very large cost value. This causes other routers to avoid this router when computing paths through the network.

The technique is backward compatible. When the Dijkstra calculation discards links with LSInfinity cost, the router is completely avoided for transit. Older routers that do not discard such links may still use them, but alternate paths will always be preferred since they have lower costs.
sections.plainLanguage: The router says my local networks have normal costs but all my links to other routers cost infinity, so you should not route through me, but you can still reach my networks.

sections.title: Compatibility with Older Routers
sections.content:
Different OSPF implementations handle infinity-cost links differently. Routers following RFC 1247 ignore links with LSInfinity cost entirely. Routers following RFC 1583 and later do not treat infinity-cost links as unreachable and will use them if necessary.

This does not create routing loops because if alternate paths exist, all routers prefer them to the infinity-cost path. If the stub router is the only way to reach a destination, routers that implement RFC 1247 skip it while RFC 1583 routers still use it. This inconsistency does not cause problems because the alternate paths and loop-free behavior are preserved.
sections.plainLanguage: Old and new routers interpret the infinity signal differently, but they both agree that other paths are better, so the network still works correctly.

references.text: Moy, J., "OSPF Version 2", STD 54, RFC 2328, April 1998.
